ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
An astronaut stands at a height $h$ on the surface of a planet and throws a small ball horizontally with an initial velocity $v_{0}$. The displacement of the ball when it lands is $x$. The radius of the planet is $R$, and the gravitational constant is $G$. The rotation of the planet is not considered.

1. The gravitational acceleration on the surface of the planet.
2. The first cosmic velocity of the planet

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: An astronaut stands at a height $h$ on the surface of a planet and throws a small ball horizontally with an initial velocity $v_{0}$. The displacement of the ball when it lands is $x$. The radius of the planet is $R$, and the gravitational constant is $G$. The rotation of the planet is not considered. 1. The gravitational acceleration on the surface of the planet. 2. The first cosmic velocity of the planet
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: From the text, the ball is thrown horizontally with initial speed v0, and the vertical drop before landing is h. The given displacement magnitude from launch to landing is x. Let the horizontal range be L. The displacement components form a right triangle, so x^2 = L^2 + h^2, hence L = sqrt(x^2 - h^2). Since horizontal velocity is constant, the flight time is t = L/v0 = sqrt(x^2 - h^2)/v0. Vertically, the ball starts with zero vertical velocity and falls distance h, so h = (1/2) g t^2. Substituting t gives h = (1/2) g (x^2 - h^2)/v0^2, so g = 2h v0^2/(x^2 - h^2). The first cosmic velocity near the planet surface satisfies v1 = sqrt(gR). Substituting g gives v1 = v0 sqrt(2hR/(x^2 - h^2)).
